paragraphs.text: The burden of Nineveh.
The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. [1]

About a century and a half earlier God had sent the prophet Jonah to warn Nineveh, the great city, of its destruction because of its corruption, and when the king and the people offered repentance, He forgave them and pardoned them. But soon they returned to their sins and fell into a worse state, until it was called "the bloody city" (Nah 3:1). And since they persisted in their evils in a hideous manner, He did not send them a prophet, but sent them a prophecy announcing the destruction that would come upon the city. As it is written in the book of Jeremiah: "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; if it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them" (Jer 18:9-10).
This prophecy was fulfilled at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus (Ahsuerus) or Xerxes.

* The meaning of the word "burden" is something of this kind: when God wishes to give the prophets insight, He often brings about a rapture of joy, causing a sudden change in their minds, so that in this state they receive knowledge of the future with deep fear. He calls it a "burden," and afterward the grace of the Spirit, where it seizes the mind of the prophet suddenly, turning him by a vision to the clear revelation of what is happening. He says the same thing here also: "The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite," as though he were saying: the mind of the prophet was suddenly seized by the grace of the Spirit and turned to contemplate those matters from which he learned what the fate of Nineveh would be, a matter that was presented to his hearers as teaching about what had been shown to him.
Theodore of Mopsuestia

entries.section: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

paragraphs.text: 2 God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies. 3 The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. 4 He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth. 5 The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is lifted up at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein. 6 Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him. 7 The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him. 8 But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies.
God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth.
The LORD revengeth, and is furious.
The LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies. [2]

The prophecy came harsh and violent, yet full of tenderness and affection for the souls that cling to God. He begins by speaking of the Lord as a jealous God. This jealousy characterizes a husband toward his wife, so that he does not allow anyone to touch her or to wrong her, and it characterizes a king toward those who are subject to him in loyalty, so that he plans and works to protect them. So God's jealousy over man is a part of His love for him. He does not accept that anyone or anything should compete with Him to occupy the heart of man, His beloved.
His jealousy sometimes requires that He use the rod of discipline on man, because the latter wounds the relationship of mutual love by giving God his back and not his face.

He pours out this jealousy into the hearts of His faithful servants, so that they say with the Apostle Paul: "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ" (2 Cor 11:2).

The heart of Phinehas the priest was kindled with jealousy for the holiness of the people and the tabernacle of the congregation when Israel committed harlotry with the daughters of Moab and worshipped their pagan gods, and one of them dared to bring a Midianitish woman to his brethren and enter with her into the tabernacle of the congregation. For when the priest thrust her through, the Lord said: "Phinehas... hath turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, while he was zealous for my sake among them, that I consumed not the children of Israel in my jealousy" (Num 25:11).

Elijah the prophet also says: "I have been very jealous for the LORD God of hosts: because the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword" (1 Kgs 19:10).

"God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth" [2]; He is jealous for His believers who walk in His way, who are sincere in their love for Him, and who trust in Him. If they sin, He disciplines them out of His jealousy and His great love for them; and He is an avenger not for His own sake but to protect His children, counting everyone who takes a stand of enmity against them as taking it against Himself personally. Therefore He says: "he reserveth wrath for his enemies" on behalf of His children.

God permitted the kingdom of Assyria to carry His people into captivity to discipline them, but Assyria thought that its idols were greater than God, and so it began to mock Him; and it went on humiliating the people of God.
* God is jealous, and He does not mock anyone with scorn. He does not mock like one who boasts of his own goodness, but He is longsuffering, yet He threatens.

Tertullian * My brethren, it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the Lord. And fearful is the face of the Lord against them that do evil (Ps 34:16)... Fearful is the ear of the Lord, which hears the voice of Abel speaking through his silent blood. Fearful are His feet, which step over the doing of evil. Fearful also is His filling of the universe, where it is impossible for any place to escape the work of God (Jer 23:24), even by flying up to heaven, or going down into hell, or fleeing to the uttermost east, or hiding ourselves in the depths, at the end of the seas (Ps 139:7-8). Nahum the Elkoshite stands before me trembling when he announces the burden of Nineveh, for God is jealous, and the Lord revengeth in His wrath against those who oppose Him.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Observe, my beloved children, how the Lord our God is merciful and righteous, how compassionate and gentle with men, yet with great emphasis He "will not at all acquit the wicked" (see Nah 1:2). Although He welcomes the return of the sinner and grants him life, and leaves no room for any doubt, He does not act like one who judges harshly and utterly rejects the wicked, and refuses to give them counsel to bring them back to repentance. On the contrary, God says through Isaiah to the bishops: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, ye priests; speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem" (see Isa 40:1). Therefore it is fitting for you, when you hear these words of His, to encourage those who have sinned, to lead them to repentance, and to offer them hope. And it is not in vain that you reckon that you will share their transgressions at the expense of your love for them. Receive the penitent with joy, rejoice over them, and judge sinners with mercy and tender compassion. For if someone were walking on the bank of the river and stumbled, and you pushed him and threw him into the river instead of extending a helping hand to him, you would have committed the crime of murdering your brother.
Apostolic Canons The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked.

entries.section: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

paragraphs.text: The LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. [3]

God is slow to anger, waiting for man's repentance and return to Him. It was fitting for Assyria to realize that the victory it gained over the people of God was for the discipline of the people, so that it might take warning, abandon its idols, and believe in God, especially since they had previous experience in the days of the prophet Jonah. But instead of believing in God, Assyria used every means to treat God with contempt and blaspheme Him, and to humiliate His people in a savage manner. As the Apostle Paul says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God" (Rom 2:4-5).
God's longsuffering toward the wicked is not from any inability in power, for He is "great in power"; He delays, awaiting their repentance, and otherwise He will by no means acquit them.
"The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever" (Ps 103:6-7).

The Lord showed Moses that He is merciful out of power and love, for the LORD descended in the cloud, and passed by before him, and proclaimed: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands..." (Ex 34:5-7). And Moses made haste, and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshipped.
God is longsuffering, but He will not at all acquit, that is, He does not leave evil alone to the end. Those who persist in their evil and do not repent, He will by no means acquit.

Just as man cannot withstand whirlwinds and storms and prevent the clouds, so he cannot stand before the wrath of God in arrogance and pride, but by repentance and humility he enjoys the divine mercies.

* "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy" (Ps 103:8). Why is He so longsuffering? Why is He plenteous in mercy? Men sin and live; sins continue and life continues. Men blaspheme every day, and He makes His sun to rise on the evil and on the good (Mt 5:45). In any case, He calls to amendment, He calls to repentance, He calls by His blessing of creation; He calls by giving time for life (opportunities for repentance), He calls through the reader (of the Word in the Church), and through the preacher, and He calls through the inner thought with the rod of correction, and He calls with the mercies of consolations. He is longsuffering and merciful. But take heed lest by abusing the greatness of God's mercies you treasure up for yourself wrath against the day of wrath, as the Apostle says (Rom 2:7).

St. Augustine * Again: "And I will establish my covenant with thee; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: that thou mayest remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame, when I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord GOD" (Ezek 16:62-63). Thus by these divine words He clearly indicates what was said in another place in the phrase: "And if He cleanses you, He does not make you righteous." For even the righteous, when they return from their former state after committing a sin, do not dare to open their mouths, but say with the Apostle: "I am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God" (1 Cor 15:9).

St. Jerome * "The Lord is longsuffering, and great in power, and will certainly not at all acquit" (Mic 1:3). He does not inflict punishment (discipline) immediately and suddenly, but after great longsuffering. You, O people of Nineveh, are witnesses to that, for when you practiced repentance you found salvation; after committing many evils for a long time you did not receive punishment for them. But when a people practice evils for a long time, He inflicts punishment on the impenitent. (The meaning of "will not at all acquit" is that He does not exempt from punishment those sinners who deserve it.)

Theodoret of Cyrus "The clouds are the dust of his feet." Here is a metaphor for the speed of chariots and surpassing horses, for they raise a cloud of dust, so that it is difficult to see them. So the Lord is like one who comes from heaven in His chariot, swift as lightning, and the clouds surround Him as the dust surrounds chariots and horses.
He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers.

entries.section: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

paragraphs.text: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth. [4]

God created everything by a word, and by a word from Him He rebukes the sea and dries it, and dries up all the rivers that pour their waters into the seas. In ancient times He divided the Red Sea so that His people might cross as on dry land, and He made a way for them to cross the Jordan.

The seas and rivers, with all their powers, dry up at a word from Him, while man, in his extreme weakness, takes a stand of disobedience and rebellion against his Creator, who is longsuffering toward him and loves him!

If man thinks himself to be something, let him look at Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon, the regions marked by greenery and beautiful flowers, for they wither before the heat of summer or the frost of winter. Who then is man that he should stand before the Creator of time and the Ruler of the whole universe?
Bashan was famous for its green pastures (Joel 1:10), Carmel for its fields of wheat and vineyards, and Lebanon for its forests (Isa 33:9).

Tertullian sees here a prophecy about the Lord Christ, who rebuked the winds, so that they were stilled and the waves grew calm: [Here is a prophecy of Christ walking on the waters, which preceded His coming. The words of the Psalm were fulfilled by Christ's crossing the lake, for the Psalmist says: "The LORD is upon many waters" (Ps 29:3). When He scattered its waves, the words of Habakkuk were fulfilled, who said: "He numbers the waters as He goes" (Hab 3:10) LXX, and when He rebuked the sea and it was calm, the words of Nahum were also fulfilled: "He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry" (Nah 1:4), referring to the winds that had stirred up the sea].

entries.section: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

paragraphs.text: The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is lifted up at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein. [5]
Who can stand before his indignation?
And who can abide in the fierceness of his anger?

entries.section: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

paragraphs.text: His fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him. [6]

The divine wrath is likened to the fires of volcanoes and earthquakes that demolish rocks, melt hills, and destroy entire cities, and there is no possibility of standing before these natural phenomena. If rocks that seem firm, which no one can move, collapse before the fires of erupting volcanoes, how then will man stand before the fires of divine wrath?

"Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, mine anger and my fury shall be poured out upon this place, upon man, and upon beast, and upon the trees of the field, and upon the fruit of the ground; and it shall burn, and shall not be quenched" (Jer 7:20).
The LORD is good.
A strong hold in the day of trouble.

entries.section: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

paragraphs.text: And he knoweth them that trust in him. [7]
Lest anyone, even the Assyrians, think that God is a mighty avenger, the prophet stresses the goodness of God and His tenderness toward those who trust in Him.

When man is angry he loses his peace, his love, and his tenderness, but God in His wrath against evil is full of tenderness. The prophet Habakkuk says in his prayer: "in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2). In His wrath against evil He waits to have mercy on the sinner if he reveals his true longing for repentance. While the wicked are terrified of meeting with God, those who trust in Him sing, saying: "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him" [7]. The righteous see in the power of God a consuming fire that protects them, able to save them; He surrounds them and keeps them from every fiery dart aimed against them. St. Peter says: "The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished" (2 Pet 2:9).

* "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good" (Ps 106:1). You who commit grave sins and despair of salvation, and think that because of the gravity of your sins you cannot obtain pardon, I advise you, or rather the prophet advises you, to give thanks to the Lord, for He is good. Great are your sins, but great is the Lord who has compassion on you. Confess your sins to the Lord, repent, and do not despair of your salvation, for the Lord is merciful. Do not rely on your own strength but rely on the mercy of the Lord.

St. Jerome * "For the Lord is good," good not in the same way as the things He created are good. For God made all things very good (Gen 1:31), not only good, but also very good... If He made all these things good, what kind (of goodness) is that which made them...? How far can we speak of His goodness? Who can grasp what is in His heart, and understand how the Lord is good? Let us return to our souls, for we are not worthy to contemplate Him in Himself. And in hope that we may contemplate Him when our hearts are purified by faith, then we shall rejoice in the truth. Now, since we cannot see Him, let us look at His works so that we may not live without praising Him. Therefore I say: give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, sing to His name, for it is sweet... What is sweeter than the food of angels? How could God not be sweet, when man ate the food of angels? For men live on food that is not different. This is true, it is wisdom, it is the goodness of God, but you cannot enjoy it in the same way as the angels.

entries.section: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies. [8]

Some see in this phrase a prophecy of what would befall Nineveh from the army of the Medes and Babylon, where the army storms the city as though a flood had come upon it, and no one can stand before it. Others see that it is a prophecy of the conduct of this army when it took Nineveh by making a flood in the river that destroyed the wall of 20 furlongs (Furlongs, a measure of length equal to 220 yards or one eighth of a mile).

entries.section: 3. The destruction of the kingdom of Assyria and its army:

paragraphs.text: 9 What do ye imagine against the LORD? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time. 10 For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry. 11 There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the LORD, a wicked counsellor.
What do ye imagine against the LORD?
He will make an utter end.
Affliction shall not rise up the second time. [9]

Perhaps he is referring here to what Sennacherib and his deputy Rabshakeh did, who reproached the Lord of hosts and spoke of Him openly as a God unable to protect His people and unable to rescue them from the hand of the king of Assyria.

The prophet mocks the kingdom of Assyria, which thinks itself a great kingdom able to resist the great God in His power, and asks: What do you devise against the Lord? For your resistance is not against mortal men, but against the Almighty Lord.

"Affliction shall not rise up the second time"; for when Sennacherib king of Assyria tried to take Jerusalem, his army was destroyed and his two sons killed him on his return to his own country, so there is no room for him to repeat the attempt and try to take Jerusalem again. Some see that the meaning here is that once the army of Assyria is destroyed there is no room for destroying it again, for it does not rise again to fight anew!

* A father does not teach his son unless he loves him. And a master does not improve his disciple unless he sees in him signs of promise. When a physician comes and does not attend to the patient, this is a sign that he despairs of him. It is fitting for you to answer thus: since Lazarus received evil things in his life, I accept with joy the sufferings so that I may enjoy the glory to come for me. For affliction shall not rise up the second time (Nah 1:9).

St. Jerome * A bishop, priest, or deacon who falls into fornication, perjury, or theft is to be cut off from his priestly rank but not suspended, for Scripture says to you: [Do not take vengeance twice for the same crime with sorrow] (see Nah 1:9) LXX.

Church Canons * Here I think the ancient authorities followed the old law: "Thou shalt not take vengeance twice for the same thing" (Nah 1:9) LXX. For this reason also lay people (the people), when they are excluded from the place of the faithful, are restored from time to time to the rank from which they fell. But the deacon falls under a final penalty by being cut off from his rank, and the rank of the diaconate is not restored to him, but remains as a permanent punishment.

* Priests who commit a sin unto death are deprived of their rank, but they are not excluded from the communion of the laity (the people), for one is not punished twice for the same fault (Nah 1:9) LXX.

entries.section: 3. The destruction of the kingdom of Assyria and its army:

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry. [10]

King Sennacherib and his men, as they reproach the Lord of hosts, are reckoned like dry thorns standing before a blazing fire, or like drunkards who do not know what they utter. They are like stubble fully dry, which the fire devours with extreme speed.

It is clear that these slain soldiers (185 thousand) shared with their leader his evil spirit and his mockery of the Lord God, and therefore the angel of the Lord struck them. This appears from the prophet's words: "folden together as thorns, and drunken." Each of them was strengthening the hands of the others in evil, and stirring them up to blaspheme God, so that they became like a mass of thorns that cannot be separated from one another, which the farmer burns together with fire. And they were like a company of drunkards, each urging the rest to drunkenness and mockery.

Thorns signify the wicked, for they are like thorns that seem harmful, but are dry and soon catch fire and become helpless ashes. "But the sons of Belial shall be all of them as thorns thrust away, because they cannot be taken with hands: but the man that shall touch them must be fenced with iron and the staff of a spear; and they shall be utterly burned with fire in the same place" (2 Sam 23:6-7).
Drunkards stagger and pretend to be brave, and boast of themselves as great, rich, and strong, though a man could make them fall with the tip of his finger.
Diodorus Siculus relates that when the enemy entered Nineveh, Sardanapalus burned his famous palace, and thus the prophecy of Nahum was fulfilled that they would burn like thorns.

entries.section: 3. The destruction of the kingdom of Assyria and its army:

paragraphs.text: There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the LORD, a wicked counsellor. [11]
He directs the speech to Nineveh, from which Sennacherib came out uttering evil against the Lord, and so destroys himself as he destroys the city from which he came out.

He calls Rabshakeh the foolish counsellor who advised the men of war sitting on the wall not to trust in the Lord, for He is unable to rescue them out of the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria (Isa 36). He is a counsellor of destruction, because his reproach of the Lord of hosts led to the killing of one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army in one night by the angel of the Lord (Isa 37:36). Sennacherib himself was also killed by his two sons Adrammelech and Sharezer (Isa 37:38).

12 Thus saith the LORD; Though they be quiet, and likewise many, yet thus shall they be cut down, when he shall pass through. Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more. 13 For now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder. 14 And the LORD hath given a commandment concerning thee, that no more of thy name be sown: out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image: I will make thy grave; for thou art vile.
Thus saith the LORD:
Though they be quiet, and likewise many, yet thus shall they be cut down, when he shall pass through.
Though I have afflicted thee,
I will afflict thee no more. [12]

The kingdom of Assyria was like a razor that mowed down kingdoms as hair is shaved from the head, and therefore the punishment came that it itself would be mowed down. It is written in Isaiah: "In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard" (Isa 7:20).

Since this army had previously defeated many cities that relied on their pagan gods, they stood before Jerusalem as men in safety and peace, proud of their multitude and strength, and behold, they are "cut down" like grass, and the destroying angel passes through them and humbles them at once, and they do not rise from this destruction to fall again into a new destruction!

By saying, "Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more," the Lord reveals His purpose in discipline, which is the repentance of the sinner in humility and abasement, so that the Lord may lift him up and set him on high in glory. Therefore it is said of the Lord: "For the Lord will not cast off for ever: but though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men" (Lam 3:31-33).

By saying, "Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more," God assures King Hezekiah that He permitted him and his people this siege so that the people might recognize their fault and offer sincere repentance in a spirit of humility. And the blow that would strike the army of Assyria besieging Jerusalem would be decisive, so that Sennacherib would not besiege it again.
For now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder. [13]

The Lord assures King Hezekiah and his men that God will break the yoke of Sennacherib and his army and burst his bonds, for the army of the Assyrians was storming many of the cities and villages of Judah, doing as it pleased with them, while Jerusalem was unable to defend these places, being like a city bound and fettered. It will enjoy freedom, and the army of Assyria will not launch another attack, for its strength will fail with the killing of 185 thousand by the angel of the Lord, and the army will be as though extinct, with no power.
The yoke which Assyria laid is the tribute that Sennacherib imposed on Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:14).
And the LORD hath given a commandment concerning thee:
That no more of thy name be sown.
Out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image.
I will make thy grave; for thou art vile. [14]

The command has gone out to destroy his name, so that no one speaks of him any more as a conqueror and victor, and his reputation is scattered with the wind like dust that passes and does not return. By saying "out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image," he perhaps refers to the killing of King Sennacherib by his two sons in the house of Nisroch his god (Isa 37:38; 2 Kgs 19:37). This hideous crime showed Nisroch's inability to protect the one who worshipped him, and the people looked at this temple, defiled by the crime, and cut the images out of it and refrained from worshipping in it. Perhaps he refers here to the collapse of the kingdom of Assyria, where the enemy laid Nineveh waste and smashed the images of their gods, which they thought were the secret of their victory.

"I will make thy grave; for thou art vile": the house of Nisroch his god became a tomb for him, where he lay despised by his two sons who killed him treacherously, so that he was deprived even of filial love. Perhaps he means here the city of Nineveh, which became a grave for Assyria, since it was destroyed in a shameful manner.

When our God enters our hearts, we long that our name be sown no more, since we bear His name, and we sing, saying: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). He shatters the ego in us and establishes His divine Kingdom in us. Selfishness is buried as in a grave, and He takes away our vileness to grant us fellowship in His glories, and the heavenly ones sing: "The king's daughter is all glorious within" (Ps 45:13), and the Heavenly One Himself speaks to us: "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (Song 4:7). "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?" (Song 6:10).
Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!
O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts.
Perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee.
He is utterly cut off. [15]

As he announces to Jerusalem the loosing of her bonds, the breaking of the yoke of the army of Assyria, the destruction of its king Sennacherib, and the cutting off of the images of its gods, Nahum prophesies of what is greater, namely the salvation that the Messiah offers to the whole world. He sees in the Lord Christ the One who comes as upon the mountains to proclaim true, eternal, inward peace, reconciling mankind with the Father, turning our lives into unceasing feasts, and shattering and cutting off the enemy of good, so that he has no authority over the children of God, but he and his hosts and his devices and his works and his thoughts are cut off: "he is utterly cut off."
What are these mountains on which the feet of the herald of peace walk, if not the prophecies that prepared mankind to receive the Savior?

* Surely He brought good tidings to Zion and offered peace to Jerusalem. He goes up on a mountain, and there He spends the night in prayer (Lk 6:12). Therefore return to the prophets and learn from them His whole role. Isaiah says: "O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain" (Isa 40:9). "And they were astonished at his doctrine: for his word was with power" (Lk 4:32)... [I am present, when the hour comes, on the mountains, I bring the good news of peace, and I announce good] (see Isa 42:7). And as one of the Twelve (the minor prophets), Nahum, says: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace, hastening" (see Nah 1:15).

Tertullian * Let him who remembers the Gospel recall how He (the Lord) ascended from hell and breathed the Holy Spirit into the face of Judah, that is, the Jewish disciples, since they belong to the New Covenant, whose feast days have become spiritually renewed and cannot grow old. Moreover we have seen that the rest of the prophecy (Nah 1:14) has been fulfilled, for the Gospel destroyed "the graven image and the molten image," that is, the idols of vain gods, which are now consigned to oblivion in the grave.

St. Augustine * By speaking of the feet he means the coming of the Apostles who went about the world preaching the coming of the Kingdom of God. Their appearing enlightened mankind by showing the way to peace with God, for whom John came to prepare (Mk 1:3; Isa 40:3). This is the peace to which those who believe in Christ hasten.

Father Ambrosiaster * It is not only my words that make these things clear, but the prophet foretold it beforehand, crying out: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace" (Nah 1:15). And what is his message that he proclaimed, if not what he went on to declare to them, saying: "Keep, O Judah, thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows to the Lord. For they shall no more return to what is old. It is finished; it is utterly cut off. He has been lifted up who breathed in the face and delivered thee from affliction" (Nah 1:15; 1:2) LXX. And now: who is this who has been lifted up...? If you wish to know the truth and be rid of the claims of the Jews, look to our Savior who was lifted up and breathed into the face of His disciples, saying: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost" (Jn 20:22). For as soon as this (the crucifixion) was accomplished, the old things came to an end: the veil of the temple was rent (Mt 27:51), and the (Jewish) altar was shattered, and although the city had not yet been laid waste, the abomination of desolation (Mt 24:15) was preparing to sit in the midst of the temple, and Jerusalem and all those old ordinances were receiving their end.

* The day of the feast has drawn near to us again, in which, if we keep silent, we make it unholy, but it must be dedicated to prayer more than all days, and in it we keep the commandments. For although we are in distress from those who grieve us, and because of them we shall not tell you about this season (since it is not among His people), yet thanks be to God who comforts the sorrowful, so that we are not defeated by the evils of those who accuse us and keep silent; in our obedience to the voice of truth we cry out with you aloud on the day of the feast, for the God of all told them (Moses and Aaron) to speak to the people to keep the Passover, and the Spirit proclaims in the Psalms, saying: "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day." And the prophet cries out, saying: "O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts" (Nah 1:15).

And I am not sending you the word as though you were ignorant, but I am declaring it to those who know it, that they may realize that although some divide us from one another, God gathers us together, for we keep the feast with the same feast, and we worship the same God continually.

And we do not keep the feast as spectators, knowing that the Apostle rebukes such people, saying: "Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years" (Gal 4:10), but rather we honor this great day because of the feast, so that we may please God, all of us who serve God in every place, by our common prayers. The blessed Paul announced such a joy as near, and in this he did not announce days but the Lord for whose sake we keep the feast, for he says, "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7), so that, contemplating the eternity of the Word, we draw near to Him to serve Him.

* My dear beloved, God has brought us again to the season of the Passover, and through His tender love He has gathered us together to keep the feast. For God, who brought Israel out of Egypt, even now still calls us to the Passover, saying through Moses: "Observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the LORD thy God" (Deut 16:10), and says through the prophet: "O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows" (Nah 1:15).

For if God Himself loves the feast and calls us to it, it is not right, my brethren, to put it off or to keep it slackly, but we must come to it with zeal and joy, so that, beginning to rejoice here, our souls may long for the heavenly feast.

If we keep the feast here with vigor, we shall without doubt receive the perfect joy that is in heaven, as the Lord says: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer: For I say unto you, I will not any more eat thereof, until it be fulfilled in the kingdom of God" (Lk 22:15-16).

So we eat of it now, if it makes us understand the reason for the feast, and by our knowledge of the Savior we walk according to His grace, as Paul says: "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 5:8). For in these days the Lord died, so that we may no longer long for the works of death! He gave His life, so that we may keep our lives from the snares of Satan!

St. Athanasius the Apostolic * [Concerning monks] It befits us to observe the days mentioned in such a way that the rest may be beneficial and not harmful to the body and the soul. For the joy of any feast does not weaken the thorns of the flesh, and our savage enemy (Satan) cannot be quiet because of these days of rest. So that we may keep the traditions of the feast season, and not be subject to the rule of fasting... it is enough for us at this time to take food at the sixth hour (12 noon) instead of the ninth hour, without changing the quantity or kind of food, lest we lose the purity of body and goodness of soul that we obtained during the Great Lent...

We must be on guard with vigilance to the end, lest our souls grow faint because of temptations and we lose the purity of our chastity that we obtained, through rest and negligence at the time of the Paschal feast after continual striving throughout the Great Lent. Therefore we must not add anything to the kind or quantity of food, but even in the two names of the feasts we must abstain from these foods, lest our joy in the feast stir up in us an extremely deadly struggle because of bodily passions, and so we turn to sorrow. Then we would weep for the lost purity of our heart with the sorrow of endless remorse.

At the same time it befits us to strive lest we be rebuked with this warning: "O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows" (Nah 1:15). For if the days of the feast do not conflict with the continuance of our asceticism, we enjoy constant spiritual feasts.
Abba Theonas
Mighty are You in Your love!

1 The mace is lifted up against thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily. 2 For the LORD restoreth the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches. 3 The shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men are in scarlet: the chariots shall be with the fire of steel in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken. 4 The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings. 5 He shall recount his worthies: they shall stumble in their walk; they shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared.
The mace is lifted up against thy face.
Keep the munition.
Watch the way.
Make thy loins strong.
Fortify thy power mightily. [1]

God used Assyria as a rod of discipline for His people, but Assyria exalted itself against God and reproached Him, and used every means to practice savagery against the people of God who were under discipline. Now God sends Babylon as the hammer of the whole earth (Jer 50:23), which begins its blows upon great Nineveh openly and boldly.

He calls Babylon: "The mace is lifted up against thy face" [1], and some translate it: "He that crusheth is come up against thy face." Babylon is the axe that God uses to crush Assyria. "Thou art my battle axe and weapons of war: for with thee will I break in pieces the nations, and with thee will I destroy kingdoms; and with thee will I break in pieces the horse and his rider; and with thee will I break in pieces the chariot and his rider; with thee also will I break in pieces man and woman; and with thee will I break in pieces old man and young; and with thee will I break in pieces the young man and the maid; I will also break in pieces with thee the shepherd and his flock; and with thee will I break in pieces the husbandman and his yoke of oxen; and with thee will I break in pieces governors and the wreckage" (Jer 51:20-23).
Thus God permitted the army of the Medes and Babylon to destroy Nineveh.

On the surface it is a war between states and peoples, but in reality it is God's permission, in support of those who trust in Him and who are under discipline, and for the punishment of arrogant Nineveh. Therefore He announced to Assyria beforehand that Nineveh would be openly shattered, and that every effort to defend it would be in vain. Let Assyria put forth all its efforts to preserve Nineveh, but the decree has gone out from heaven for its destruction. Therefore he says: "Keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily," for all this will profit nothing. Let it station forces to guard its fortresses, and set watchmen in the towers to follow the enemy's attack, and let it encourage its soldiers and multiply its military resources, but let it know: "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but victory is of the LORD" (Prov 21:30). In vain does it try to enjoy victory while it resists the Lord Himself.
For the LORD restoreth the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches. [2]

The prophet declares the reason for the destructive war against Nineveh, which is that Assyria despoiled Jacob, having mistreated the captives from Israel and carried out barbarous attacks on Judah, and stood reproaching the Lord of hosts as unable to save them from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria. As they plundered they are plundered, and as they reproached the Lord of hosts shame comes upon them, and the Lord restores to His people their dignity after disciplining them.

In the Septuagint it says: "One has arisen who breathes upon thy face, delivering thee from trial" (Nah 2:2) LXX. Theodoret of Cyrus sees that this offers a kind of breathing for the salvation of man. For He had earlier breathed into Adam the breath of life (Gen 2:7); and since man lost the effect of this divine breath, the Lord Christ came to renew the image of man and to restore it in the holy Apostles, and in all the rest of the believers through the Apostles; He breathed on the face of His disciples, saying: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost" (Jn 20:12). God shattered the Assyrians with the breath of His mouth to save His people; as a type of the work of the Lord Christ, who shatters the tyrant devil with the breath of His Holy Spirit, whom He gave to His Church.
The shield of his mighty men is made red.
The valiant men are in scarlet.
The chariots shall be with the fire of steel in the day of his preparation.
And the fir trees shall be terribly shaken. [3]
Here he describes the commanders of the army of the Medes and Babylon who attack Nineveh.

"The shield of his mighty men is made red": the ancients preferred the color red for the shield; on one side, like those who raise the red flag to terrify the enemy, just like bullfighters who think they provoke the bulls with red flags. On the other side, if one is wounded and his blood is scattered on his shield, the enemy does not notice this, and so is encouraged to fight. Some see that the shields of the Assyrians were of copper, as appears from their antiquities, so that the red color of the shields of the army of the Medes and Babylon was the result of the reflection of the sun's rays on them.

"The valiant men are in scarlet," for their garments were scarlet. Xenophon says that the Medes were fond of the color red. Since scarlet is costly, it shows the wealth of the army and its capabilities.

"The chariots shall be with the fire of steel in the day of his preparation": a picture of the intensity of the attack, as the enemy's chariots move in a frenzied manner, and sparks fly like fire produced by the friction of the chariot wheels against the stones, so that the wheels are like torches from which rays of fire shoot forth.

Perhaps he also means that the enemy's chariots carry fiery torches so that they may carry on the battle by night and by day, for the war does not stop until Nineveh is completely destroyed. The soldiers of Gideon carried lamps in pitchers (Judg 7:16) to guide them and to spread terror among their enemies.
This is what God permitted at the appointed time, or in the day of his preparation, so that Nineveh might receive the fruit of its deeds.

"And the fir trees shall be terribly shaken": the enemy's army is like towering cypresses, shaking continually to terrify Assyria. Perhaps he wishes to express how fiercely the army moves, as the cypress trees shake with the ground under the feet of the soldiers because of their multitude and their constant powerful movement.
The chariots shall rage in the streets.
They shall justle one against another in the broad ways.
They shall seem like torches.
They shall run like the lightnings. [4]

It shows the capability of the swift-moving, new military chariots; they are shining, appearing as fiery torches and burning lamps among the trees that surround the roads, because of the reflection of the sun on them. They move with force like lightning, as in a state of frenzy.
He shall recount his worthies.
They shall stumble in their walk.
They shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared. [5]

Some see that the speech here concerns the king of Assyria, who counts the commanders and heroes of his army and brings the valiant among them to lead the situation in the defense of Nineveh, but they stumble in their walk, and all their efforts fail. Others see that the speech here concerns Nebuchadnezzar, who reminds the commanders of his army, the heroes, not to draw back however strong the fortresses of Nineveh may be. As they hasten toward its wall they stumble, but they do not despair; rather they dig trenches to protect them from the arrows of those besieged inside Nineveh. And they complete the siege with the utmost speed.

6 The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved. 7 And Huzzab is discovered, she is brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts. 8 And Nineveh is of old like a pool of water: but now they flee away. "Stand, stand!" but none looketh back. 9 Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture. 10 She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather redness. 11 Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions, where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion's whelp, and none made them afraid?
The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved. [6]

The gates of Nineveh were open on the river Tigris, on which the city was built. The wall on the side of the Tigris, on the western side of Nineveh, was 4,530 yards long. On the south, north, and east there were huge water moats that could easily be filled with water from the Khosru; the people of Nineveh filled all the moats and channels with water to surround the city on every side, so that the enemy could not cross over to them with their chariots and horses. Diodorus says that in the third year of the siege, when a great flood occurred, 20 furlongs (4,400 yards) of the walls of Nineveh collapsed, and the king burned himself, his palace, his concubines, and his wealth, and the enemy entered through the breached wall. Thus the prophecy of the prophet Micah was fulfilled: "The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved" [6]; for the heart of the king and those with him in the palace melted from fear, and they resorted to suicide by fire.

In the Septuagint it says: "The mountains have fallen" (Nah 2:6) LXX. St. Ambrose sees that the mountains point to the great things by which man is puffed up and exalts himself against God. For whoever has faith as a grain of mustard seed says to the mountain that it be cast into the sea, and it is cast (Mt 17:20).
And Huzzab is discovered.
She is brought up.
And her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts. [7]

Huzzab is the name of the queen of Nineveh who fled from the fire, since it was recorded of the king alone that he was burned with fire. The queen was brought before the enemy and he led her away captive in shame and disgrace, and her maids bewailed her state. Some see that "Huzzab" is a symbol of the city of Nineveh itself.
The maids have nothing before them but continual lamentation like the unceasing cooing of doves, and beating on their breasts as a sign of intense grief and of inability to act.
And Nineveh is of old like a pool of water, but now they flee away.
Stand, stand!
But none looketh back. [8]

Nineveh was crowded with inhabitants like a pool full of water (Isa 8:7; Jer 51:13; Rev 17:15), but all are unable to act; rather they are fleeing, and some commanders try to rouse the spirit of courage in them, crying out, saying: "Stand, stand," but none looks back, for they have lost all hope of salvation, and so they flee in every direction without restraint.
Take ye the spoil of silver.
Take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture. [9]
Nineveh gathered its wealth of gold, silver, and precious treasures from the annual tribute, from spoils, and from its huge trade (Nah 3:16; Ezek 27:23-24).
The king burned his palace with all the treasures in it, but the enemy took possession of the gold, silver, and treasures of the city and of its great men.
She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins.
And the faces of them all gather redness. [10]

A bitter picture of what Nineveh comes to in ruin and terror. The rich city has become emptiness, even void and waste. And she who dominated many nations has a fainting heart and loosened knees, and cannot stand or flee. The faces of her soldiers and people turn red, as though inflamed with the fire of bitterness and grief. Some translate it: "and the faces of them all are pale."
Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions?
Where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion's whelp, and none made them afraid? [11]
The Assyrian monuments were often adorned with images of lions in various forms, among them the winged lion with a human head.

Nineveh, as the capital of the greatest state at that time, was reckoned the dwelling of the lions and the feedingplace of the cubs, where the king and queen walked as a lion and lioness in a forest. Now the surrounding nations stand asking: Where is great Nineveh with her might? Where are her lions, the mighty men of war and her great men? She was like a lions' den full of spoils coming from all the nations subject to her! Assyria tyrannized and plundered for the sake of its capital. Now the capital loses everything, and it is said of her: "The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing" (Ps 34:10).
The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin. [12]
Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts.
And I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions: and I will cut off thy prey from the earth, and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard. [13]

If the kingdom of Assyria prides itself on its forces and its army that never knew defeat, the One who rises against it is "the Lord of the heavenly hosts," or "the Lord of the forces." It is He who vindicates the oppressed, defends the humiliated, and grants victory to the right.

Behold, the chariots of Assyria cannot endure the fires of divine wrath, and they burn from the mere smoke before the flames reach them. This kingdom has no more standing, for its young lions die by the sword, so there is no hope for kings (lions) to rise, nor will it acquire spoils any more, and there are no messengers to send to threaten the nations around it. What Assyria did to the nations is done to it; its deed returns upon its own head (Obad 15).
Who will restore my dignity but You?
* The enemy robbed me of my inner glory!
Instead of heaven, the enemy reigned over my depths.
He robbed me of my life and glory, and plundered all my gifts and energies for his own account.
This is the dangerous Assyria that humbled my soul.
* Behold, Your hand moves to restore the excellency of Jacob!
I see Your hands stretched out on the Cross, waiting for the whole world to embrace it with love, and to free it from the devil and all his hosts!
* Behold, You lead the battle Yourself, O my God!
What enemy can stand before You?
Your chariots are mighty and effective, they run like the lightnings.
You occupy my heart to give it surpassing victory.
You drive the enemy out of it, and take from him all that he seized.
He goes out shattered, with no power or strength!
* He thought himself a lion, preying with no one to restrain him!
His cubs hungered and lacked.
His forces were shattered and he fell like lightning from the heaven of our hearts.
Glory to You, who give glory to those who trust in You.

1 Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not; 2 The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the prancing horses, and of the jumping chariots. 3 And the horsemen rise up, the flame of the sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of wounded, and a great number of slain; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses.
Woe to the bloody city!
It is all full of lies and robbery.

The prey departeth not. [1] 1. The trial of Nineveh begins with the first charge against it, which is that it is a "bloody city." It shed the blood of many innocents, and delighted in torturing captives and cutting off their limbs in a savage manner.

* "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity" (Ps 5:5), whether they be slaves or free or an emperor, whoever the worker of iniquity may be. For God reckons persons His friends not on the basis of honors, but on the basis of virtue, as you see.

St. John Chrysostom St. Augustine comments on the Psalmist's words: "But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men..." (Ps 55:23), asking us to beware of the murderers of souls more than of those who shed the blood of bodies. [Those who separate themselves from unity kill souls by leading them astray spiritually, not shedding blood bodily].

And in his comment on the Psalmist's words: "And shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: and the land was polluted with blood" (Ps 106:38), St. Augustine sees that perhaps the Psalmist does not mean here the offering of human sacrifices. Truly this custom existed among many nations, especially in the worship of Baal, where a family would sometimes offer its children as human sacrifices to appease the gods. But what the Psalmist means here is the Israelites' participation in pagan worship and its abominations, so that they bequeathed this crime to their children, who grew up practicing it, and in this way the fathers killed the souls of their sons and daughters, and deprived them of the holy life and of fellowship with God. This killing is more hideous than the killing of the body, for in it there is deprivation of eternal life. 2. The second charge: its use of lying and deceit, for it justified its continual attacks by claiming that it was keeping justice and protecting it, and so it put on a deceptive garment with which it covered its evil intentions. Through lying and deceit the heart is drawn into many evils, for it is not frank with itself so as to live pure and clean, loving God and men, but hides its evils and corruption with deceitful words.

* "Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing" (Ps 5:6)... God hates evil, utterly abhors and rejects it. Now the Psalmist calls those who live in evil speakers of lies (of falsehood). Those who have vain aims, who are addicted to pleasures, gluttonous and greedy. Here you see that he reckons all these in the class of liars.

He abhors the bloody and deceitful man (Ps 5:6). He points here to the murderer, the schemer of evil, the deceiver, who utters one thing on his lips and carries another in his heart. He who is a wolf in a lamb's garment, there is none worse than he. In other words, while an open enemy can be confronted, the one who hides his evil while actually practicing it is not easily discovered, and so he commits many crimes; therefore Christ warns us of the coming of such people: "which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves" (Mt 7:15).

St. John Chrysostom 3. The third charge is robbery and plunder, for they did not cease to steal what belongs to others, and without being satisfied they seek to rob those they prey on. The Psalmist Solomon says: "He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight" (Ps 72:14).

* Let us lament with Nahum, and say with him: [Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness] (see Jer 22:13; Nah 3:1). Rather, let us grieve over them as Christ did in His days when He said: [Woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your reward and your consolation] (see Lk 6:24). I ask: "Let us not cease to grieve in this way, and if the matter is unseemly, let us lament over the lukewarmness of our brethren. Let us not weep with a loud voice over one who has actually died, but lament over the thief, the covetous, the miser, and the greedy."
St. John Chrysostom The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the prancing horses, and of the jumping chariots [2]

The prophet takes us into the midst of the battle to hear the sound of the whips with which the drivers of the war chariots urge the horses to hurry, and the sounds of the wheels of the exceedingly swift chariots, the leaping of the horses, and the jumping of the chariots.
And the horsemen rise up, the flame of the sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of wounded, and a great number of slain; and there is none end of their corpses.
They stumble upon their corpses. [3]

He continues his picture of the battle, for the horsemen rise up to fight so as to leap upon their horses to kill the enemies, and the gleaming swords flash like flame, and the spears aimed at the people of Nineveh glitter. Many are wounded, and the slain are without number; there is no one to gather the corpses, nor does anyone care, but the warriors stumble over them because of their abundance and the flood of blood flowing from them.

4 Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts. 5 "Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame. 6 And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock. 7 And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?"
Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts. [4]

She did not take warning from what happened to her army when the angel of the Lord killed 185 thousand in one night, and therefore this happens in Nineveh on the day of her utter ruin. 4. The fourth charge is harlotry. Earlier he pictured Nineveh as the lion that is torn apart and whose cubs hunger and are scattered; here he pictures her as a lewd harlot who urges the nations to pagan worship and its abominations. She prides herself on her beauty and her power to seduce. She destroyed the nations by her harlotry.

* Reproof is a rebuking discipline, and the divine Teacher used it in Jeremiah, saying: "Thou hadst a whore's forehead, thou refusedst to be ashamed before all, and thou didst not call me to thy house, I am thy father, and the lord of thy virginity" (see Jer 3:3-4). "Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot in the cup of enchantment" (see Nah 3:4). And with an all-embracing and complete skill, after calling the virgin by the scandalous, shameful name of harlotry, He calls her to return to an honored life by filling her with feelings of shame.

St. Clement of Alexandria 5. The fifth charge: she is the mistress of witchcrafts, or its lady, selling families through her witchcraft. For all that occupied the kingdom of Assyria was to rule the world and bring all the nations under its feet. It did not stop at using war, plunder, and rapine, but resorted also to witchcraft, as the harlot does with her enchantment, hunting young men by bodily allurement and enslaving them.
Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame. [5]

Nineveh thought herself the beautiful lady of the world who captures the nations by her witchcraft and harlotry, so that all submit to the worship of her gods and practice abominations with her. But since God hates evil, He deals with her as a harlot, and exposes her corruption, so that she is like one stripped of the harlot's garments that attract to corruption. This is also what the prophet Isaiah prophesied of Babylon, which afterward followed the same course as Nineveh: "for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate... uncover thy veil, gather up the train, uncover the leg, pass over the rivers; thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen" (Isa 47:1-3). She loses not only her deceitful beauty and her enchantment, but appears in shame and disgrace, loathsome and ugly. Her tricks are exposed to the nations, her evil plans are uncovered, and her weakness and corruption appear. "And I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame" [5]. All realize that she is neither strong nor the lady of the world as she claimed.
And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock. [6]
That city with which the states longed to ally themselves has become a laughingstock and a joke to all.
And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say:
Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her?
Whence shall I seek comforters for thee? [7]
Instead of the nations' taking refuge in her out of fear of her authority, they look at what has befallen her, and flee from her, for she is not fit even to dwell in.

From the severity of the complete destruction there is none to bemoan her, for there is no hope of her restoration any more, and there are no comforters, for all gloat over her. Everyone who sees her is terrified at what has befallen her, and his tongue cannot utter a word of comfort.

entries.section: 3. She becomes an example like others:

paragraphs.text: 8 Art thou better than populous No Amon that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea? 9 Cush and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers. 10 Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains. 11 Thou also shalt be drunken: thou shalt be hid, thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy.
Art thou better than populous No Amon that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea? [8]

Lest Nineveh think, or those who hear the prophecy think, that it is impossible for it to be fulfilled, the prophet gives an example of a town that was strong and secure, and when it walked in evil and persisted in resisting God, the divine wrath came upon it: it is "No Amon."
No Amon: some see that it is Thebes, which bore this name, and is in Upper Egypt, and its meaning is "the portion or possessions of Amon." And Amon is the Egyptian god Jupiter.

It appears that King Sargon of Assyria is the one who struck No Amon; and as Assyria triumphed over Thebes in spite of all its powers and resources, so the turn comes to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, to lose its glory and be destroyed by the Babylonians.

"That was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea." Thebes lay on both banks of the river Nile, east and west, and huge water channels surrounded it, so it was like one in safety, as Nineveh was, for we saw earlier how waters surrounded it, preventing enemy armies from reaching its walls.
In the days of Homer, Thebes was famous for its hundred gates.
Its ruins and remaining monuments still measure 27 miles around, and contain within them the famous temples of Luxor and Karnak.
By the sea he means here "the river Nile," and to this day it is so called in Upper Egypt.
Cush and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite.

entries.section: 3. She becomes an example like others:

paragraphs.text: Put and Lubim were thy helpers. [9]

Cush: most often what is meant by it is the region of Yemen, and sometimes what is meant is southern Egypt, that is, Nubia, and also Ethiopia. Cush derived its strength and wealth from trade and military aid. It was a support for No Amon.

Put and Lubim: two neighboring kingdoms west of Egypt in North Africa, namely Cyrene and Libya, and Egypt depended on them greatly, and No Amon obtained supplies from them, and so lived securely, like a queen sitting on her throne.

entries.section: 3. She becomes an example like others:

paragraphs.text: Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains. [10]

Since No Amon sat in safety, proud of her strength and wealth, supported by many lands in the south and north, and surrounded by waters to protect her from any attacks, she did not expect any fall, and behold, she goes into exile, taken captive. Her pride and her strength betrayed her, and her children were dashed in pieces. They cast lots for her great men, for it was the custom of the victorious commanders, when they took a great city, to seize its great men, and then cast lots for them so as to distribute these great men as slaves to the commanders. Instead of golden chains and the display of pomp and greatness, these became naked, barefoot slaves, bound with iron chains, dragged to their country in shame and disgrace.
Thou also shalt be drunken.
Thou shalt be hid.

entries.section: 3. She becomes an example like others:

paragraphs.text: Thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy. [11]

What befell the city of No Amon befalls Nineveh, and from the horror of it her inhabitants become drunk, deranged in mind, drinking from the cup of God's wrath against them. As it was said to Jerusalem: "which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out... Therefore hear now this, thou afflicted, and drunken, but not with wine..." (Isa 51:17, 21). And in the prophet Jeremiah it says: "For thus saith the LORD God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it. And they shall drink, and be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. Then took I the cup at the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to drink, unto whom the LORD had sent me" (Jer 25:15-17).

Origen has a beautiful comment on the phrase: "Every bottle shall be filled with wine" (Jer 13:12). Every man is like a bottle filled with wine, but there are two kinds of wine: a good wine, which is the wine of the love of God that makes the soul drunk, so that it melts in love for God, and lives contemplating Him, as though it were drunk with this love. This wine is prepared by Wisdom: "Wisdom hath... mingled her wine... Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled" (Prov 9:1, 5). But the evil wine that fills the wicked is like the wine of Sodom and Gomorrah: "For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah: their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter: their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps" (Deut 32:32-33). He also sees that God holds in His right hand the cup of our good works to grant us His blessings, and in His left hand a cup to discipline us until we return to Him.

And St. Augustine speaks to us of the wine of the love of God, saying: [Have not those whose hearts have been changed become drunk? He says: "all the sinners of the earth drink" (Ps 75:8). But who are those who drink the wine? Sinners drink so that they may no longer remain sinners, but that they may be justified, and not be punished].

"Thou shalt be hid" [11], that is, Nineveh hides herself in shame because of the disgrace and fear that have overtaken her, for she is unable to face the enemy; and she seeks a stronghold to protect her, but she has no support.

12 All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater. 13 Behold, thy people in the midst of thee are women! The gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies: the fire shall devour thy bars. 14 Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln. 15 There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts! 16 Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and fleeth away. 17 Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are. 18 Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust: thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them. 19 There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?
All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater. [12]

The prophet likens her to fig trees when the firstripe figs appear on them, which, when the wind shakes them, drop all the figs that are on them. So Nineveh will not be able to repel the enemy, but her children fall with great speed to be eaten!
Behold, thy people in the midst of thee are women.
The gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies.
The fire shall devour thy bars. [13]
Her army will be like women unable to defend themselves, and the gates of the city open to the enemy without resistance, and the fires blaze in her bars.
Draw thee waters for the siege.
Fortify thy strong holds.
Go into clay, and tread the morter.
Make strong the brickkiln. [14]

In mockery he asks Nineveh to store water and provisions for the period of the siege so that she may not die of thirst and hunger. For although the city is built on the river Tigris and waters surround it through the river and the water moats, its army and all its inhabitants are unable to go out and drink from them.
He asks her to repair her fortresses, and they rebuild every fortress in it or repair it. But all this goes to nothing, and she is like one in mire, unable to be rid of it.
There shall the fire devour thee.
The sword shall cut thee off.
It shall eat thee up like the cankerworm.
Make thyself many as the cankerworm.
Make thyself many as the locusts! [15]

He calls her not to rely on the multitude of her inhabitants and the men of her army, for they become like the cankerworm and the locusts, destructive insects, which cannot stand before the blazing fire, nor stand before the sword.
Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven.
The cankerworm spoileth, and fleeth away. [16]
Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day.
But when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are. [17]

Because of her geographical location on the river Tigris with water channels around her, she was a huge commercial country, but when wrath comes and the enemy rises against her, she turns from a city crowded with merchants into a field laid waste by locusts too many to count. Her great men become like locusts on a cold day, who, when the sun rises, fly, and do not know where they are going.

Perhaps he means that the foreign merchants who came to Nineveh for trade, and had acquired great wealth, when they see the enemy coming take their wealth and flee. These are the ones whom Nineveh thought would support her in her time of distress, but like locusts they soon fly away from her, hoping to find a safe place.

And some see that by the fleeing locusts he means here the hired soldiers who guard the walls from outside, for being hirelings they see the enemy coming and flee, and do not know where they are going. As the Lord Christ says: "The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep" (Jn 10:31).
Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria.
Thy nobles shall dwell in the dust.
Thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them. [18]

The king of Assyria thought he was under the protection of shepherds and commanders, mighty men of valor, but he was surprised by the prophet awakening him and saying to him: "Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria" [18]. His great men lay down, for they were killed and fell in the streets in the dust, while his people fled to the mountains in terror, and there is none to gather them.
There is no healing of thy bruise.
Thy wound is grievous.
All that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually? [19]

The prophet closes his speech by picturing the state of Nineveh as one who is broken with none to mend the break, and wounded with no healing for the wound, for there is no return to the building of Nineveh, nor to the rise of the state of Assyria anew. And since she was violent with all the nations that fell under her hand, they began to mock her, clapping their hands, as they see the fruit of her evil and reproach her.
Let Nineveh be shattered, and let the new Jerusalem arise in me!
* The enemy crept into my heart, and set up a kingdom for himself in me.
Drive out the king of Assyria, and make a public example of him by Your Cross.
Strip him of his authority, and establish Your Kingdom within me!
* Remove from me what the enemy planted in me.
It is foreign to my nature which You gave me.
Remove all love of injustice, and all lying and deceit, remove from me every evil desire, and all vainglory.
Expose me before myself, that I may return to You, O You who are all love and mercy.
* I confess to You my weakness and my inability to resist, but You are my stronghold!
You are the heavenly Physician who heal my wounds, and mend every break in my bones!
* Instead of the wine of sin that robs me of my balance, give me the wine of Your heavenly wisdom, that I may be drunk with Your love, and sing of Your mercies.
Let me forget the world and all its allurements, and enjoy the earnest of Your heavens!
